title: Department of War Daily Briefing
description: Secretary-level initiatives, acquisition, Golden Dome, operations and policy across the Department of War.
readFirst: Covers Oct. 20–22, and keeps the Oct. 14–15 items that are still the standing picture. New: a Reuters dispatch that the IRGC says seven vessels were hit or struck mines near Hormuz; Hegseth's Guyana agreement and a Florida Air National Guard special tactics squadron; Project Agincourt's roadmap for Autonomous Warfare Command; and his Oct. 20 Dayton speech naming Project Meridian and a reconciliation bill of at least $350 billion. No new Golden Dome appropriation was found. The fiscal 2027 request is still mostly in reconciliation that has not been enacted.

items.headline: In Dayton, Hegseth names Project Meridian and says a reconciliation bill of at least $350 billion is the priority
items.summary: Speaking Oct. 20 at Sierra Nevada Corporation in Dayton on the Arsenal of Freedom tour, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said the department had just launched a Future of Warfare initiative called Project Meridian, which he said demands all-domain connectivity and rapid technological advances at the edge. He tied that to the Autonomous Warfare Command announced at Quantico, which he described as a four-star combatant command with service-like authorities. He said the department has no higher priority than passage of a reconciliation bill of at least $350 billion, and that the administration is asking for a $1.5 trillion defense investment. He also said the department will pass a full audit before 2028, and described five- to seven-year orders for companies that invest in new plants.

items.headline: Hegseth and Guyana's president sign an enhanced defense partnership at the Pentagon
items.summary: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Guyanese President Mohamed Irfaan Ali signed what the Pentagon called a landmark agreement at the Pentagon on Oct. 21, creating an enhanced defense partnership. Hegseth said shared challenges include narco-terrorism and military influence from outside the Western Hemisphere, and that the two countries would push back by exercising what he called President Trump's corollary to the Monroe Doctrine. He said the United States will intensify combined training in multidomain operations and in air interdiction. On critical minerals, he said Guyana's pursuit of a memorandum of understanding with the United States will bolster a shared defense industrial base.

items.headline: Hegseth directs a new Air National Guard special tactics squadron in Florida
items.summary: The Department of War said Oct. 21 that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signed a memo directing a new Air National Guard Special Tactics Squadron in Florida. Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell said the squadron would sit with the U.S. Special Operations Command and Air Force Special Operations Command community at Hurlburt Field and MacDill Air Force Base. The release says the move is meant to bolster combat controller, pararescue, and special reconnaissance capabilities by using Air National Guard personnel. It describes the location, next to USSOCOM at MacDill and AFSOC at Hurlburt, as a way to concentrate training and mission execution.

items.headline: Hegseth hosts Britain's defense secretary and presses a NATO 3.0 rebalance
items.summary: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth met United Kingdom Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting at the Pentagon on Oct. 15, Streeting's first Washington visit since taking office in July. Hegseth described NATO 3.0 as Europeans taking primary responsibility for their own conventional defense so the United States can shift attention, including toward the Pacific. The Pentagon readout says Hegseth urged more British defense spending, discussed the review of U.S. force posture in Europe, asked London to keep supporting a durable peace in Ukraine, and raised security in the Strait of Hormuz. Hegseth also thanked Streeting for communication about threats to U.S. forces in Britain, including the security incident at RAF Fairford that led the U.S. to withdraw bombers.

items.headline: Project Agincourt publishes an operational roadmap for Autonomous Warfare Command
items.summary: The Department of War said Oct. 21 that Project Agincourt leaders Owen West and Senior Chief Max Strasiser sent an open letter to the joint force and industry partners with an operational roadmap for the Autonomous Warfare Command. The release quotes them that urgency does not excuse imprecision. They described a combat-first model that pushes procurement decisions and dollars to frontline warfighters. The department said success is measured by how fast an operational problem receives a fielded, scalable solution, not by paperwork milestones.

items.headline: Autonomous Warfare Command still needs Congress before its Oct. 1, 2027 target
items.summary: At AUSA on Oct. 14, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told the autonomy panel the effort is not another procurement effort. Hegseth's Sept. 30 direction creates Autonomous Warfare Command as a four-star combatant command with service-like authorities to scale drones and robotics. Stars and Stripes reports that standing the command up by Oct. 1, 2027 requires the Pentagon to work with Congress on the necessary legislation. Service secretaries from the Army, Air Force and Navy were on the stage. Additional detail on the command was not shared in the session.

items.headline: Almost all of the fiscal 2027 Golden Dome request still sits in reconciliation
items.summary: No new appropriation for Golden Dome was found this week. CSIS's tracker of the fiscal 2027 request says the department asked for $17.1 billion of a $17.9 billion Golden Dome total inside the reconciliation package rather than discretionary funding, and that the direct reporting program manager has warned a lack of fiscal 2027 funding would stop further development. Axios reported Oct. 7 that senators questioned cost and coverage at a Sept. 29 hearing. The Congressional Budget Office has estimated as much as $1.2 trillion over 20 years. Gen. Michael Guetlein has said the system stays inside a $185 billion figure. Those estimates disagree, and the reconciliation bill that would fund the request has not been enacted.

items.headline: IRGC says four vessels were hit and three more struck mines near Hormuz
items.summary: A Reuters dispatch published by Al-Monitor on Oct. 22 said Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy reported that four vessels involved in what it called illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were hit at the same time and caught fire on Wednesday, after its forces tracked them. The IRGC said three more vessels collided with mines west of the Strait of Hormuz. It warned the U.S. military that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. The dispatch does not include an independent confirmation of the strikes.

items.headline: Iran says Hormuz stays restricted until Washington accepts its terms
items.summary: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iraqi state television that the Strait of Hormuz will not be open to everyone until there is an agreement on the waterway, The National reported Oct. 21. Indirect talks continue through Pakistan and Qatar. In a Financial Times article the same week he wrote that further escalation around Hormuz would put civilian lives and the global economy at risk, and that he sees little reason to expect progress while Washington threatens more violence. The National also reported, citing Fox News and two U.S. officials, that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit are heading to the region, on the order of 10,000 sailors and Marines by the end of November, which would be a third carrier.

items.headline: Hegseth says the U.S. is prepared to go further against Iran if Trump directs it
items.summary: Middle East Eye reported Oct. 21 that Hegseth told reporters the United States is prepared to contribute any way necessary so Iran never gets a nuclear weapon, and that if Tehran will not give up the program and the president asks to go further, the department is prepared. The National reported that Hegseth met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, Oct. 19, while the two sides discussed whether to resume major combat operations before the U.S. midterms. Iranian officials told Reuters, The National said, that Tehran is preparing for possible renewed attacks and sees little chance of a diplomatic breakthrough before the U.S. election.

items.headline: Trump cancels a plan to livestream the Fort Hood shooter's execution
items.summary: NBC News reported Oct. 15 that President Trump overruled a plan by Hegseth to livestream the firing-squad execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shootings. The execution itself remained scheduled for December. Al Jazeera reported the same day that Trump wrote the event will not be streamed and that immediate family members of victims would be able to view it. The reversal followed objections from Republicans and the public.
